title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf node.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4].
hints: The depth of a node is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees' depths; recurse and take the max.

test_cases.explanation: The longest path is 3 -> 20 -> 15 (or 7), so the depth is 3.
An empty tree has depth 0.

title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return its minimum depth: the number of nodes along the shortest path from the root down to the nearest leaf node (a leaf has no children).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^5].
hints: A node with only one child is NOT a leaf, so you cannot stop there -- you must continue down the existing child.

test_cases.explanation: The nearest leaf is node 9, reached in 2 nodes.
There is no left child anywhere, so you must follow the single right chain down to the leaf.

title: Symmetric Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (symmetric around its center).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000].
hints: Compare the left subtree against the MIRROR of the right subtree: left.left with right.right, and left.right with right.left.

test_cases.explanation: The tree mirrors itself around the root.
The inner values (3) are both on the right, breaking the mirror.

title: Same Tree
description:
Given the roots of two binary trees `p` and `q`, check whether they are structurally identical and every corresponding pair of nodes has the same value.

The tree is given as `p`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000. The same applies to `q`.
constraints: The number of nodes in each tree is in the range [0, 100].
hints: Two trees match only if the roots match AND both pairs of subtrees match, recursively.

test_cases.explanation: The 2 is a left child in `p` but a right child in `q`.

title: Invert Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, invert it (swap every node's left and right subtree) and return the resulting tree.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000. Return the inverted tree serialized the same way.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100].
hints: Swap a node's two children, then recurse into both (now-swapped) subtrees.

test_cases.explanation: Every left/right pair swaps: 2<->7, then 1<->3 and 6<->9.

title: Balanced Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is height-balanced: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000].
hints: Compute height bottom-up in a single DFS pass; short-circuit (or just record) as soon as any subtree's imbalance is found instead of recomputing heights repeatedly.

test_cases.explanation: The left subtree of the root has height 3 while the right has height 1.

title: Path Sum
description:
Given the root of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return true if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that the values along that path sum to `targetSum`.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000].
hints: A leaf is a node with no children at all -- subtract the node's value from the target as you descend, and only check at true leaves.

test_cases.explanation: No root-to-leaf path sums to 5.
Node 2 is the only leaf, and 1 + 2 != 1.

title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return the average value of the nodes on each level, from top to bottom.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
The answer for each level is guaranteed to fit in a double.
hints: A level-order (BFS) traversal naturally groups nodes by level -- sum and count each level's queue snapshot before moving to the next.

test_cases.explanation: Level averages are 3, 14.5, and 11.

title: Range Sum of BST
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and two integers `low` and `high`, return the sum of values of all nodes whose value lies in the inclusive range [`low`, `high`].

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 2*10^4].
hints: Use the BST property to prune: only recurse left if `low` could still be beaten, only recurse right if `high` could still be beaten.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, return the length (in number of edges) of the diameter: the longest path between any two nodes, which may or may not pass through the root.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: At every node, the best path THROUGH it is left-height + right-height; track the global max of that while computing heights bottom-up.

test_cases.explanation: The longest path is 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 or 5 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3, with 3 edges.

title: Cousins in Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree and the values of two different nodes `x` and `y`, return true if the two nodes are cousins: they are at the same depth but have different parents.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 100].
hints: Record each node's (depth, parent value) in one pass, then just compare the two records.

test_cases.explanation: 4 is at depth 2, 3 is at depth 1 -- different depths.
Both at depth 2, with different parents (2 and 3).
Same depth but same parent (2), so not cousins.

title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer `k`, return true if there exist two distinct nodes whose values sum to `k`.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: A single DFS with a hash set works just like the array version of Two Sum -- the BST ordering isn't even required.

test_cases.explanation: No two distinct node values sum to 28.
There is only one node, so no pair of DISTINCT nodes exists.

title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree, return the minimum absolute difference between the values of any two distinct nodes.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10^4].
hints: An in-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, so the minimum difference is always between some pair of IN-ORDER-ADJACENT values.

test_cases.explanation: In-order: 1,2,3,4,6 -- the smallest gap is 1 (e.g. 1 and 2, or 2 and 3, or 3 and 4).

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on its right side. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom (the last node visited on each level).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100].
hints: A level-order (BFS) traversal makes this direct: on each level, the rightmost node dequeued is the one that's visible.

test_cases.explanation: From the right you see 1, then 3 (2 is hidden behind it), then 4.
On the last level, only 4 exists, so it's the visible one (3 is on level 2, hidden by nothing but 4 is deeper on the left).

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree are strictly greater.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: Checking only a node's immediate children against each other is not enough -- pass down a valid (low, high) range from each ancestor.

test_cases.explanation: The right subtree's node 4 is less than the root 5, which violates the BST property.
Node 6 is in the root's right subtree but is less than the root, violating the property.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
description:
Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer `k`, return the `k`-th smallest value among all node values in the tree (1-indexed).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: An in-order traversal of a BST yields values in strictly increasing order -- the k-th value visited is the answer.

test_cases.explanation: In-order: 2,3,4,5,7,8,9 -- the 3rd value is 4.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree and the values of two nodes `p` and `q` known to both exist in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (a node can be a descendant of itself).

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10^5].
p and q both exist in the tree.
hints: Recurse into both children; if a node's left AND right subtree each report finding one of p/q, that node itself is the LCA.

test_cases.explanation: 5 and 1 are the root's two direct children, so the root (3) is their LCA.
4 is a descendant of 5, so 5 is its own ancestor here.

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
description:
Given the root of a binary tree, a node X is called good if, on the path from the root to X, there is no node with a value greater than X's value. Return the number of good nodes.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^5].
hints: Carry the maximum value seen so far on the current root-to-node path as you DFS down.

test_cases.explanation: The good nodes are 3 (root), 4, 5, and the second 3 -- 4 total.

title: House Robber III
description:
The houses in a neighborhood form a binary tree; a thief cannot rob two directly connected houses (a node and its parent) on the same night without alerting the police. Given the root of the tree with each node's value being the amount of money in that house, return the maximum total amount that can be robbed.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4].
hints: For each node compute two values bottom-up: the best total if this node IS robbed, and the best total if it is NOT.

test_cases.explanation: Rob 3 (root) + 3 + 1 = 7, better than robbing both 2 and 3 (level 2) = 5.
Robbing 4's two children (1 and 3) plus the root's other child 5 gives 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

title: Path Sum III
description:
Given the root of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return the number of downward paths (paths that move strictly from a node to any of its descendants, without going back up) whose node values sum to `targetSum`. A path does not need to start at the root or end at a leaf.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 1000].
hints: Track running prefix sums root-to-current-node in a hash map (like the array 'subarray sum equals k' trick) -- a path summing to targetSum ending at the current node exists once for every earlier prefix equal to (current prefix - targetSum).

test_cases.explanation: The three paths are 5->3, 5->2->1, and -3->11.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
description:
A path in a binary tree is any non-empty sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes in the sequence is connected by an edge; a node can appear at most once, and the path does not need to pass through the root. Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum of any path.

The tree is given as `tree`, a level-order (breadth-first) array where -100000 marks a missing child; trailing -100000s after the last real node are omitted, and no real node value is ever -100000.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 3*10^4].
hints: For each node, the best path THROUGH it uses at most one branch into each child (clamped at 0 to ignore negative contributions); but the value a node can RETURN to its parent may only extend into one side.

test_cases.explanation: The best path is 2 -> 1 -> 3, summing to 6.
The best path is 15 -> 20 -> 7, summing to 42, ignoring the negative root.

title: Sum of Distances in Tree
description: There is an undirected, connected tree with `n` nodes labeled 0 to n - 1, and `n - 1` edges. Given `n` and the array `edges` where each `edges[i] = [ai, bi]` denotes an edge, return an array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` is the sum of the distances (in edges) between node `i` and every other node in the tree.
constraints: The given input represents a valid tree.
hints: First compute answer[0] and every subtree size with one post-order DFS from node 0.
Then re-root: moving the root from a node to one of its children changes the answer by -size[child] + (n - size[child]).

test_cases.explanation: For node 0: distances are 1+1+2+2+2 = 8.

title: Number of Islands II
description: You are given an `m x n` grid that starts entirely as water. You are also given `positions`, where `positions[i] = [ri, ci]` turns the cell at `(ri, ci)` into land (if it is already land, this operation does nothing). Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the number of islands (maximal 4-directionally connected groups of land) after the i-th operation.
hints: Union-Find handles this online: adding land starts a new island (+1), then union with any already-land 4-directional neighbor (-1 per successful union).

test_cases.explanation: After the last operation (1,1) touches both (0,1) and (1,2), merging every land cell so far into one single island.
Repeating an already-land position doesn't change the count.

title: Minimize Malware Spread
description: You are given a network of `n` nodes as an `n x n` adjacency matrix `graph`, where `graph[i][j] == 1` means nodes `i` and `j` are directly connected. A subset `initial` of nodes starts infected with malware; infection spreads through direct connections until every reachable node from any infected node is infected. If you remove exactly one node from `initial` (which also removes it from the network entirely, along with its edges), return the node whose removal minimizes the final count of infected nodes; if several nodes tie, return the smallest node index.
constraints: All entries in initial are distinct.
hints: Find the connected components with Union-Find first.
Only removing a node that is the SOLE infected node in its component can ever reduce the final infected count -- and it reduces it by exactly that component's size.

test_cases.explanation: Nodes 0 and 1 are in the same component, so removing either leaves the other still infecting it -- return the smaller index, 0.
Each node is its own isolated component of size 1 -- ties broken by smallest index.

title: Shortest Path to Get All Keys
description: You are given an `m x n` grid `grid` where each cell is one of: `.` (empty), `#` (wall), `@` (starting point), a lowercase letter (a key), or an uppercase letter (a lock that needs the matching lowercase key to pass through). You start at `@` and can move in 4 directions one cell at a time. Return the minimum number of moves needed to collect all the keys, or -1 if it's impossible. There is exactly one of each key/lock letter present, and at most 6 keys.
constraints: Keys are lowercase letters starting from 'a'; a lock is the matching uppercase letter.
hints: BFS over the state (row, col, bitmask of collected keys) rather than just (row, col) -- the same cell can be worth revisiting once you're carrying different keys.

test_cases.explanation: 8 moves collects both keys a and b.
The lock A blocks the only path to key a.

title: Sliding Puzzle
description: On a 2x3 board there are 5 tiles numbered 1 to 5 and one empty slot represented by 0. A move consists of choosing 0 and swapping it with one of its 4-directionally adjacent tiles. Given the board's starting configuration `board` (a 2x3 array), return the minimum number of moves needed to reach the solved state `[[1,2,3],[4,5,0]]`, or -1 if it is unsolvable.
hints: Flatten the 2x3 board into a length-6 tuple and BFS over all reachable permutations from the start state -- there are only 720 possible states at most.

test_cases.explanation: Swapping 0 and 5 solves it in 1 move.
This starting arrangement can never reach the solved state (odd permutation).
Already solved.

title: Word Search II
description: Given an `m x n` grid of characters `board` and an array of strings `words`, return every word from `words` that can be formed by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, without reusing the same cell twice within one word. Return the found words sorted alphabetically.
constraints: board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter.
hints: Build a trie of all target words first, then run one DFS per starting cell, walking the trie alongside the board so shared prefixes are explored only once.

test_cases.explanation: 'oath' and 'eat' can both be traced through adjacent cells.
Would require reusing the cell containing 'b'.

title: Palindrome Pairs
description: Given an array of unique strings `words`, return all pairs of distinct indices `[i, j]` such that concatenating `words[i] + words[j]` forms a palindrome. Return the pairs in any order.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: For each word, check every way of splitting it into a prefix/suffix: if the suffix is a palindrome, its reverse-prefix could pair AFTER it; if the prefix is a palindrome, its reverse-suffix could pair BEFORE it. A hash map from word to index makes each lookup O(1).

test_cases.explanation: (0,1): abcddcba, (1,0): dcbaabcd, (2,4): llssssll, (3,2): slls.

title: The Skyline Problem
description: A city's skyline is the outer contour of the silhouette formed by all its buildings viewed from a distance. Given `buildings` where each `buildings[i] = [lefti, righti, heighti]` describes a rectangular building, return the skyline as a list of "key points" `[x, height]` sorted by `x`, where each key point marks the start of a new horizontal segment of the skyline's outline (the last point always has height 0, marking the end).
hints: Sweep left-to-right over every building's left and right edge; keep a max-heap of "currently active" heights (lazily removing ones whose building has already ended) and emit a new key point whenever the current max height changes.

test_cases.explanation: The classic seven-key-point skyline example.
Two adjacent buildings of the same height merge into one continuous segment.

title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
description: Given an `m x n` grid `grid` where each cell is 0 (empty) or 1 (obstacle), and an integer `k`, return the minimum number of steps to walk from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell (moving in 4 directions), where you are allowed to eliminate at most `k` obstacles along the way. Return -1 if no such path exists.
hints: BFS over the state (row, col, obstacles eliminated so far), not just (row, col) -- reaching the same cell having eliminated fewer obstacles is strictly better and worth re-exploring.

test_cases.explanation: Eliminating one obstacle lets you reach the bottom-right in 6 steps.
Even with 1 elimination the destination is unreachable.
A 1x1 grid: start and end are the same cell.

title: Number of Restricted Paths From First to Last Node
description: There is a weighted, undirected, connected graph with `n` nodes labeled 1 to n and edges given by `edges`, where `edges[i] = [ui, vi, weighti]`. Let `distanceToLastNode(x)` be the length of the shortest path from node `x` to node `n`. A restricted path is a path from node 1 to node `n` such that `distanceToLastNode` is strictly decreasing along every consecutive pair of nodes on the path. Return the number of restricted paths from node 1 to node `n`, modulo 10^9 + 7.
constraints: There is at most one edge between any two nodes, and no self-loops.
hints: First run Dijkstra FROM node n to get every node's shortest distance to n.
Then count paths with memoized DFS from node 1, only stepping to neighbors strictly closer (by that distance) to n -- this graph of allowed steps is automatically a DAG.

test_cases.explanation: The three restricted paths are 1->3->5, 1->2->3->5, and 1->4->5.

title: Last Stone Weight
description: You are given an array of integers `stones` representing stone weights. On each turn, pick the two heaviest stones and smash them together: if they have equal weight, both are destroyed; otherwise the lighter is destroyed and the heavier's new weight is the difference. Repeat until at most one stone remains. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
hints: A max-heap gives you the two heaviest stones in O(log n) each round.

test_cases.explanation: Equal stones fully destroy each other, leaving nothing.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
description: Design is replaced here by pure computation: given an initial array `nums`, an integer `k`, and a sequence `stream` of values added one at a time (in order), return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the k-th largest element among all values seen so far (the initial `nums` plus `stream[0..i]`) after `stream[i]` is added.
hints: Keep a min-heap of size k of the k largest values seen so far; its top is always the k-th largest.

test_cases.explanation: After adding 3 the 3rd largest of {4,5,8,2,3} is 4; then 5,10,9,4 in turn.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
description: Given a sequence `stream` of integers added one at a time (in order), return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the median of all values seen so far (`stream[0..i]`) immediately after `stream[i]` is added.
hints: Maintain two heaps: a max-heap of the smaller half and a min-heap of the larger half, rebalanced after every insert so their sizes differ by at most 1.

test_cases.explanation: After 2: median 2.0. After 2,3: median 2.5.

title: Moving Average from Data Stream
description: Given a sequence `nums` of integers added one at a time (in order) and a window size `size`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the moving average of the last `size` values ending at `nums[i]` (or of all values so far, if fewer than `size` have arrived).
hints: Keep a running sum and a queue of the values currently in the window; pop from the front once the window exceeds `size`.

title: Number of Recent Calls
description: Given a strictly increasing array `pings` of request timestamps (in milliseconds), return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the number of requests (including `pings[i]` itself) that occurred in the inclusive time window [`pings[i]` - 3000, `pings[i]`].
constraints: pings is sorted in strictly increasing order.
hints: Keep a queue of timestamps still within the window; pop from the front while the oldest entry falls more than 3000ms behind the current one.

test_cases.explanation: At t=3002, pings 100, 3001, 3002 are all within [2, 3002].

title: My Calendar I
description: You are given a list of proposed events `bookings`, processed in order, where each `bookings[i] = [start, end]` represents a half-open time interval [start, end). A booking is only added to the calendar if it does not overlap any PREVIOUSLY ACCEPTED booking. Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is true if `bookings[i]` was accepted, false otherwise.
hints: Two half-open intervals [s1,e1) and [s2,e2) overlap exactly when s1 < e2 AND s2 < e1 -- check each new booking against every already-accepted one.

test_cases.explanation: [15,25) overlaps the accepted [10,20); [20,30) does not.
Half-open intervals sharing only an endpoint don't overlap.

title: Corporate Flight Bookings
description: There are `n` flights numbered from 1 to n. You are given an array of bookings `bookings`, where `bookings[i] = [firsti, lasti, seatsi]` means `seatsi` seats were reserved on every flight from `firsti` to `lasti` (inclusive). Return an array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` is the total number of seats reserved on flight `i + 1`.
hints: Instead of adding seatsi to every flight in the range (too slow), add it once at `first` and subtract it once just after `last` in a difference array, then take a running prefix sum.

test_cases.explanation: Flight 2 is covered by all three bookings: 10+20+25=55.

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
description: Given an integer array `nums` that does not change, and a list of range queries `queries` where each `queries[i] = [left, right]`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the sum of `nums[left..right]` inclusive.
hints: Precompute a prefix-sum array once; each query then answers in O(1) as prefix[right+1] - prefix[left].

test_cases.explanation: Sum of indices 0..2 is -2+0+3=1.

title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
description: Given a 2D matrix `matrix` that does not change, and a list of queries `queries` where each `queries[i] = [row1, col1, row2, col2]` describes the rectangle with upper-left corner `(row1, col1)` and lower-right corner `(row2, col2)`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the sum of all elements inside that rectangle.
hints: Build a 2D prefix-sum table once (with a padding row/column of zeros); each query then answers in O(1) via inclusion-exclusion of 4 corners.

test_cases.explanation: The first region sums the classic 8-cell block to 8.

title: Minimum Area Rectangle
description: Given an array of distinct points `points` on the X-Y plane, return the minimum area of a rectangle formed from four of these points whose sides are parallel to the X and Y axes. If no such rectangle exists, return 0.
hints: Group points by their x-coordinate. Two columns that share the same pair of y-values (y1, y2) form a valid rectangle; track the last x-coordinate seen for each y-pair and take the smallest resulting area.

test_cases.explanation: The corners (1,1),(1,3),(3,1),(3,3) form a rectangle of area 4; (2,2) is unused.
Two rectangles are possible; the smaller has area 4.

title: Largest 1-Bordered Square
description: Given a binary matrix `grid`, return the area of the largest square subgrid whose BORDER (the four edges only, not necessarily the interior) is filled entirely with 1's. If no such square exists, return 0.
hints: Precompute, for every cell, how many consecutive 1's extend left and how many extend up.
For a candidate square of side k with bottom-right at (r,c), its border is all 1's exactly when the top-right and bottom-left corners each have at least k consecutive 1's in the right directions.

test_cases.explanation: The full 3x3 border of 1's gives area 9.
No 2x2 or larger square fits in a single row.

title: Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target
description: Given a matrix `matrix` and an integer `target`, return the number of non-empty submatrices whose elements sum to `target`.
hints: Fix a pair of columns (c1, c2); collapsing every row's elements between those columns into one running sum reduces the problem to 'count subarrays summing to target' (a hash map of prefix-sum counts) on that 1D array.

test_cases.explanation: Four single-cell 0's each count as their own submatrix.

title: Two Out of Three
description: Given three integer arrays `nums1`, `nums2`, and `nums3`, return a sorted array of all values that appear in at least two of the three arrays (each qualifying value appears exactly once in the answer, regardless of duplicates in the inputs).
hints: Convert each array to a set first, then a value qualifies if it belongs to at least 2 of the 3 sets.

test_cases.explanation: 2 appears in nums1 and nums2; 3 appears in all three.
No value repeats across two different arrays.

title: Find Common Characters
description: Given a string array `words`, return an array of all characters that show up in every string in `words`, including duplicates: if a character occurs `k` times in every string, it should appear `k` times in the answer. Return the result sorted alphabetically.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Keep a running per-character minimum count across all words (intersect frequency tables one word at a time).

test_cases.explanation: 'l' appears twice in every word, and 'e' and 'a' once each.
No character is common to both.

title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
description: Given a circular integer array `nums` (the end connects back to the beginning), return the maximum possible sum of a non-empty subarray, where the subarray may wrap around from the end of the array back to the start.
hints: The best subarray is either a normal (non-wrapping) one, found with Kadane's algorithm, OR a wrapping one, whose sum equals total_sum minus the MINIMUM subarray sum (found the same way with a min-Kadane).
Special case: if every number is negative, the minimum-subarray trick would wrongly produce an empty wrap-around subarray -- just return the best normal subarray in that case.

test_cases.explanation: The best subarray is [3], sum 3.
Wrapping around (5 + 5) beats any non-wrapping subarray, giving 10.
All negative -- the best is the single largest element, -2.

title: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
description: Given an integer array `nums`, find the shortest contiguous subarray that, if sorted in place, would make the whole array sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the length of that subarray (0 if the array is already sorted).
hints: Compare `nums` against a fully sorted copy of itself: the first and last positions where they differ mark exactly the boundary of the subarray that needs sorting.

test_cases.explanation: Sorting indices 1..4 (6,4,8,10) is enough to sort the whole array.

title: Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array
description: You are given an array of strings `nums` and an integer `k`, where each string represents a non-negative integer that may be far too large to fit in a normal 32/64-bit integer type. Return the string representing the k-th largest integer in the array (numeric order, not lexicographic order).
constraints: nums[i] has no leading zeros unless it is "0" itself.
hints: You can't just parse these as native integers -- they may overflow. But you CAN compare two digit-strings numerically by first comparing lengths, then lexicographically if lengths are equal.

test_cases.explanation: Numeric order is 3, 6, 7, 10 -- the 4th largest (i.e. smallest) is '3'.

title: Product of the Last K Numbers
description: Numbers are appended one at a time, forming the array `nums` in the order given. Given `nums` and an integer `k`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of the last `k` numbers appended up to and including `nums[i]` -- or 0 if fewer than `k` numbers have been appended yet.
hints: A running prefix PRODUCT works like a prefix sum, except a 0 anywhere in the window breaks the usual division trick -- reset the running product whenever a 0 is appended.

test_cases.explanation: The first index has fewer than 2 numbers so far (0). Every window that still contains the 0 also gives 0. Once the window is [2,5] the product is 10, then [5,4] gives 20.

title: Partition Array Into Three Parts With Equal Sum
description: Given an array of integers `arr`, return true if it is possible to split it into three non-empty contiguous parts (in the original order, covering every element) such that all three parts have the same sum.
hints: The total sum must be divisible by 3 first. Then greedily close off the first part as soon as a running sum hits total/3, then the second part the same way; what's left must equal total/3 too.

test_cases.explanation: Total is 6, target 2 per part, but no split achieves three parts of sum 2.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Move All Balls to Each Box
description: You have `n` boxes in a row, numbered 0 to n - 1. A binary string-like array `boxes` is instead given directly as the indices `p` that currently contain exactly one ball each (`p` may repeat an index if that box holds more than one ball). Moving a ball one position left or right costs 1 operation. Return an array `answer` of length `n`, where `answer[i]` is the minimum total number of operations needed to move every ball to box `i`.
hints: Moving every ball to box i costs sum(|p[j] - i|) over all balls -- there's no shortcut needed for n <= 2000, a direct double loop is fast enough.

test_cases.explanation: Moving both balls to box 1 costs |0-1|+|1-1|=1.

title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
description: Given an array `nums`, return true if it was originally sorted in non-decreasing order and then possibly rotated some number of positions (including zero positions, i.e. it may already be sorted).
hints: Walk the array treating it as circular (wrap the last element back to the first) and count how many times an element is greater than the one after it -- a valid rotated-sorted array has at most one such 'drop'.

test_cases.explanation: This is [1,2,3,4,5] rotated -- only one drop, from 5 to 1.
There are two drops (2->1 and 4->2 wrapping), so it isn't a rotation of a sorted array.

title: Find the Highest Altitude
description: A biker starts at altitude 0 and rides `n` points, where `gain[i]` is the net altitude change between point `i` and point `i + 1` (so `gain` has length n - 1 for n points, with the biker starting at point 0). Return the highest altitude reached at any point.
hints: The altitude at each point is just the running prefix sum of `gain`, starting from 0 -- track the max as you go.

test_cases.explanation: Altitudes are 0,-5,-4,1,1,-6 -- the highest is 1.

title: Count Items Matching a Rule
description: You are given a collection of items described by three parallel arrays `types`, `colors`, and `names` (so item `i` has type `types[i]`, color `colors[i]`, and name `names[i]`), along with `ruleKey` and `ruleValue`. An item matches the rule if `ruleKey` is "type", "color", or "name" and the item's corresponding field equals `ruleValue`. Return the number of items that match the rule.
hints: Map ruleKey to the matching parallel array once, then just count matches on that field.

test_cases.explanation: Only the lenovo computer is silver.

title: Number of Steps to Reduce a Number to Zero
description: Given an integer `num`, return the number of steps needed to reduce it to 0, where in each step: if the current number is even, you divide it by 2; otherwise, you subtract 1 from it.
hints: Simulate directly -- num is small enough that even the naive loop runs in well under a million steps.

test_cases.explanation: Already 0, so 0 steps.

title: Number of Equivalent Domino Pairs
description: Given an array of dominoes `dominoes` where `dominoes[i] = [a, b]`, two dominoes `dominoes[i]` and `dominoes[j]` are equivalent if `dominoes[i]` can be made equal to `dominoes[j]` by possibly reversing it (so [a,b] is equivalent to [b,a]). Return the number of pairs `(i, j)` with `i < j` for which `dominoes[i]` and `dominoes[j]` are equivalent.
hints: Normalize each domino to (min, max) and count how many times each normalized form has been seen -- every new occurrence pairs with all previous ones of the same form.

test_cases.explanation: [1,2] and [2,1] are the only equivalent pair.
All three are equivalent to each other: C(3,2)=3 pairs.

title: Count Equal and Divisible Pairs in an Array
description: Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of pairs `(i, j)` with `0 <= i < j < nums.length` such that `nums[i] == nums[j]` and `(i * j)` is divisible by `k`.
hints: The input size is tiny -- a direct O(n^2) check of every pair is intended.

test_cases.explanation: The qualifying pairs are (0,6), (2,3), (2,4), (3,4).
Only pair (0,1): i*j = 0, and 0 is divisible by any k.

title: Verify Alien Dictionary
description: In an alien language, the 26 lowercase letters are ordered according to some string `order` (a permutation of 'a' to 'z'). Given a list of words `words` supposedly written in that language, return true if `words` is sorted lexicographically according to `order`.
constraints: All characters in order are unique.
hints: Build a map from character to its rank in `order`, then compare each adjacent pair of words the same way you would with normal alphabetical order, just using the new ranks.

test_cases.explanation: 'h' comes before 'l' in this order, so 'hello' < 'leetcode'.
'd' comes after 'l' in this order, so 'word' > 'world'.
'app' is a prefix of 'apple', so 'apple' must NOT come first.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
description: Given two strings `s` and `p`, return an array of all the start indices of `p`'s anagrams in `s`, sorted in ascending order.
constraints: s and p consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Slide a fixed-size window of length |p| across s, tracking a character-count map incrementally instead of recomputing it from scratch each time.

test_cases.explanation: The substrings starting at 0 ('cba') and 6 ('bac') are anagrams of 'abc'.
p is longer than s, so no anagram can fit.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
description: Given a string `s`, sort it in decreasing order of character frequency (the character appearing most often comes first). If two characters have the same frequency, order them alphabetically. Return the resulting string.
constraints: s consists of uppercase and lowercase English letters and digits.
hints: Count each character's frequency, then sort the distinct characters by (-frequency, character) so ties break alphabetically, and repeat each one that many times.

test_cases.explanation: 'e' appears twice, 'r' and 't' once each -- 'eert' (or 'eetr'), and with the alphabetical tie-break this reference solution gives 'eert'.

title: Count Binary Substrings
description: Given a binary string `s`, count the number of non-empty substrings that have the same number of consecutive 0's and 1's, with all the 0's grouped together and all the 1's grouped together within the substring. Substrings occurring multiple times are counted once per occurrence.
hints: Run-length encode s into consecutive group sizes (e.g. '00110' -> [2,2,1]); every adjacent pair of groups contributes min(group1, group2) valid substrings.

test_cases.explanation: No 1's exist to balance the 0's.

title: Repeated DNA Sequences
description: A DNA sequence is a string made up only of the characters 'A', 'C', 'G', and 'T'. Given a DNA string `s`, return all 10-letter-long substrings that occur more than once, sorted alphabetically (each qualifying substring appears once in the answer).
hints: Slide a window of length 10 across s, tracking every substring seen so far in a hash set; any substring seen a second time belongs in the answer (add it only once).

test_cases.explanation: 'AAAAACCCCC' and 'CCCCCAAAAA' both repeat.
Exactly 10 characters -- only one substring exists, so it can't repeat.

title: Group Shifted Strings
description: Two strings are considered a "shifting sequence" of each other if every letter in one can be shifted (cyclically, 'z' wraps to 'a') by the SAME fixed amount to obtain the other (e.g. "abc" -> "bcd" -> "xyz" are all in one group). Given an array of strings `strings`, group all strings that belong to the same shifting sequence and return the number of groups formed.
constraints: strings[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Normalize each word to a canonical key by shifting it so its first letter becomes 'a' (computing every character's offset from the first, mod 26); words in the same group share the same key.

test_cases.explanation: Groups: {abc,bcd,xyz}, {acef}, {az,ba}, {a,z} -- 4 groups.
az shifts to za only by different per-letter amounts, so they are two separate groups.

title: Minimum Swaps to Make the String Balanced
description: You are given a string `s` of length `2n` containing only the characters '[' and ']', with exactly `n` of each. A string is balanced if every prefix has at least as many '[' as ']'. In one swap you may exchange the characters at two (not necessarily adjacent) positions. Return the minimum number of swaps needed to make `s` balanced.
hints: Track the running balance (+1 for '[', -1 for ']'); the largest deficit it ever reaches tells you how many misplaced ']' you're carrying -- each swap fixes two units of that deficit.

test_cases.explanation: One swap of the two outer characters gives '[][]'.
Already balanced.

title: Check if a String Can Break Another String
description: Given two strings `s1` and `s2` of the same length, string `s1` can break string `s2` (or vice versa) if there is a permutation of `s1` such that every character in it is greater than or equal to the character at the same position in `s2`. Return true if either string can break the other.
constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Sort both strings, then check position-by-position: either s1 dominates s2 everywhere, or s2 dominates s1 everywhere.

test_cases.explanation: Sorted, s2='axy' and s1='abc' -- s2 dominates position-by-position ('a'>='a','x'>='b','y'>='c').

title: Longest Happy Prefix
description: A "happy prefix" of a string is a non-empty proper prefix that is also a suffix (excluding the whole string itself). Given a string `s`, return its longest happy prefix, or an empty string if none exists.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: This is exactly the KMP failure function: fail[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that's also a suffix of it. The answer is s[:fail[n-1]].

test_cases.explanation: 'l' is both a prefix and a suffix of 'level'.
No proper prefix of 'leetcode' is also a suffix.

title: Longest Duplicate Substring
description: Given a string `s`, return the longest substring that occurs at least twice in `s` (the two occurrences may overlap). If there are multiple longest duplicated substrings, return the one whose first occurrence starts earliest; if none exists, return an empty string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Binary search on the answer's length L: for a fixed L, use rolling hashes (Rabin-Karp) to check in O(n) whether any length-L substring repeats.
If a repeat exists for length L, try longer; otherwise try shorter.

test_cases.explanation: 'ana' appears twice (overlapping), and is the longest such substring.
No substring repeats.

title: Reverse String II
description: Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, reverse the first `k` characters of every `2k` character block, counting from the start of the string. If fewer than `k` characters remain in a block, reverse all of them; if between `k` and `2k` remain, reverse only the first `k` and leave the rest as-is.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Step through the string in strides of 2k, and within each stride reverse only its first min(k, remaining length) characters.

test_cases.explanation: Blocks of 4: reverse 'ab'->'ba', leave 'cd', reverse 'ef'->'fe', leave 'g'.

title: UTF-8 Validation
description: Given an integer array `data` representing a sequence of bytes (each value is in [0, 255], i.e. only the lowest 8 bits are meaningful), return true if it is a valid UTF-8 encoding. A valid UTF-8 character is 1 to 4 bytes long: a 1-byte character starts with `0`; a multi-byte character's first byte starts with `N` ones followed by a zero (`110`, `1110`, or `11110` for 2, 3, or 4 total bytes), and every continuation byte starts with `10`.
hints: Read the leading bits of the first byte of each character to determine how many total bytes it should occupy, then verify every following byte in that character starts with the '10' continuation pattern.

test_cases.explanation: 197 is 11000101 (a 2-byte lead), 130 is 10000010 (a valid continuation), then 1 is a standalone 1-byte character.
235 is 11101011 (a 3-byte lead) but only one continuation byte (140) follows before 4, which isn't a valid continuation byte.
11111010 doesn't match any valid lead-byte pattern.

title: Word Pattern II
description: Given a pattern `pattern` and a string `s`, return true if `s` can be segmented into substrings such that there is a BIJECTIVE mapping from each character in `pattern` to a non-empty substring of `s` (the same character always maps to the same substring, different characters always map to different substrings, and the concatenation of the mapped substrings, in order, equals `s`).
constraints: pattern and s consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Backtrack character-by-character through the pattern: if the current character is already mapped, its mapped word must match next; otherwise try every possible next substring length and recurse, undoing the choice on failure. Maintain the mapping in both directions to enforce the bijection.

test_cases.explanation: a -> 'red', b -> 'blue' works consistently.
No consistent bijective assignment exists.
a and b would have to map to the same substring 'a', breaking the bijection.

title: Valid Palindrome III
description: Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, return true if `s` can be turned into a palindrome by deleting at most `k` characters from it.
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.
hints: The minimum number of deletions to make s[i..j] a palindrome is a classic interval DP: if the ends match, it's the same subproblem on s[i+1..j-1]; otherwise it's 1 + the cheaper of dropping either end.
Compare that minimum against k.

test_cases.explanation: Deleting 'b' and 'e' leaves 'acdca', a palindrome.
Needs at least 2 deletions to become a palindrome.

title: Text Justification
description: Given an array of words `words` and a target line width `maxWidth`, format the text into lines of exactly `maxWidth` characters each, fully left-and-right justified: pack as many words as possible per line, and distribute extra spaces as evenly as possible between words, with earlier gaps getting one more space than later gaps when they can't split evenly. A line with only one word is left-justified with trailing spaces. The last line is left-justified with single spaces between words and padded with trailing spaces to width `maxWidth`.
hints: Greedily pack words onto a line while they fit; once adding the next word would exceed maxWidth, distribute the remaining space among the gaps of the CURRENT line (extra spaces go to the leftmost gaps first).

test_cases.explanation: The classic three-line justified paragraph example.

title: Maximum Score After Splitting a String
description: Given a binary string `s`, split it into two non-empty substrings at some position (a left part and a right part). The score of a split is the number of 0's in the left part plus the number of 1's in the right part. Return the maximum achievable score over all possible splits.
hints: Precompute the total count of 1's; then scan the split point left to right, maintaining a running count of 0's seen on the left and 1's remaining on the right in O(1) per step.

test_cases.explanation: Splitting after index 1 ('0' | '11101') gives 1 zero + 3 ones = 4.
No zeros exist, so the best is all four 1's on the right after a 1-char left split.

title: Path Crossing
description: Given a string `path` of characters 'N', 'S', 'E', 'W' representing unit moves on an infinite 2D grid starting at the origin, return true if the path ever visits the same point twice (including returning to the origin).
hints: Track visited coordinates in a hash set as you simulate each move, starting with the origin already marked visited.

test_cases.explanation: N->E->S ends at (1,0), never revisiting a prior point.
After N, E, S, W you're back at (0,0), which was already visited.
This path returns to the origin at the end.

title: Distinct Subsequences II
description: Given a string `s`, return the number of distinct non-empty subsequences of `s`, modulo 10^9 + 7.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Track, for each of the 26 letters, the count of distinct subsequences ENDING in that letter. When you see a new occurrence of a letter, its new count becomes (sum of all 26 counts) + 1, overwriting the old count for that letter -- this naturally avoids re-counting duplicates.

test_cases.explanation: The 7 distinct subsequences are a, b, c, ab, ac, bc, abc.
The 6 distinct subsequences are a, b, ab, ba, aa, aba.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
description: Given a string `s`, a partition of `s` splits it into a sequence of contiguous substrings, each of which is a palindrome. Return the total number of distinct ways to partition `s` such that every substring is a palindrome.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.
hints: Precompute which substrings s[i..j] are palindromes with an O(n^2) DP.
Then count ways with dp[j] = number of valid partitions of the prefix ending right before index j, summing dp[i] over every i such that s[i..j-1] is a palindrome.

test_cases.explanation: The two partitions are [a,a,b] and [aa,b].
Only [a,b] works -- 'ab' itself isn't a palindrome.

title: Permutation Sequence
description: The set of all permutations of the numbers 1 to n, when listed in lexicographic order, forms a sequence. Given `n` and `k`, return the k-th permutation sequence (1-indexed) directly, without generating all of them.
hints: Each choice of the first digit fixes (n-1)! permutations after it -- so k // (n-1)! (0-indexed) tells you exactly which remaining digit to place first. Repeat with the shrinking digit pool and factorial.

test_cases.explanation: The permutations of {1,2,3} in order are 123,132,213,231,312,321 -- the 3rd is 213.

title: Stone Game IV
description: Alice and Bob take turns (Alice first) removing a non-zero perfect square number of stones from a pile that starts with `n` stones. A player who cannot make a move (0 stones left on their turn) loses. Assuming both play optimally, return true if Alice wins.
hints: dp[i] = true if the player to move with i stones remaining can force a win.
dp[i] is true if there EXISTS a perfect square k*k <= i such that dp[i - k*k] is false (leaving the opponent in a losing state).

test_cases.explanation: Alice takes the only stone (1 = 1^2) and wins immediately.
Alice takes all 4 stones (4 = 2^2) and wins immediately.
Alice can only take 1 stone, leaving 1 for Bob, who then wins.

title: Super Pow
description: Given a positive integer `a` and a very large positive integer `b` (too large to fit in a normal integer type, so it's given as an array of its decimal digits, most significant digit first), return `a^b mod 1337`.
constraints: b does not contain leading zeros unless b itself is [0].
hints: Process b's digits left to right: after each new digit d, the accumulated result becomes (result^10 * a^d) mod 1337 -- this mirrors how the exponent's value grows digit by digit.

title: K-th Smallest Prime Fraction
description: You are given a sorted (ascending), distinct array of integers `arr` and an integer `k`. For every pair `i < j`, consider the fraction `arr[i] / arr[j]`. Return the k-th smallest such fraction, as an array `[numerator, denominator]`.
hints: Binary search on the fraction VALUE itself (between 0 and 1): for a candidate value x, a two-pointer sweep counts how many fractions arr[i]/arr[j] are <= x in O(n). Narrow the search until the count matches k exactly, tracking the largest qualifying fraction seen.

test_cases.explanation: All fractions in order: 1/5,1/3,2/5,1/2,3/5,2/3 -- the 3rd smallest is 2/5.

title: Subarrays with K Different Integers
description: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of contiguous subarrays that contain exactly `k` distinct values.
hints: 'Exactly K' is hard to slide a window on directly, but 'at most K' is easy. exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1).

test_cases.explanation: There are 7 subarrays with exactly 2 distinct values.
Every one of the 6 subarrays has exactly 1 distinct value.

title: H-Index II
description: Given an array of integers `citations`, sorted in ascending order, where `citations[i]` is the number of citations a researcher received for their i-th paper, return the researcher's h-index: the maximum value `h` such that the researcher has at least `h` papers with at least `h` citations each.
constraints: citations is sorted in ascending order.
hints: Since the array is sorted, binary search for the smallest index mid where citations[mid] >= (n - mid) -- everything from that index onward gives the h-index n - mid.

test_cases.explanation: 3 papers have at least 3 citations each (3,5,6), and h=4 fails since only 2 papers have >=4.

title: Sort an Array
description: Given an array of integers `nums`, sort it in ascending order and return it. Implement an O(n log n) comparison-based algorithm (e.g. merge sort or heap sort) rather than relying on the fact that a library sort would trivially pass.
hints: Merge sort: split the array in half, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves in linear time.
Quicksort with a randomized pivot also averages O(n log n), but has an O(n^2) worst case without care.

title: Count Pairs With XOR in a Range
description: Given an integer array `nums` and two integers `low` and `high`, return the number of pairs `(i, j)` with `0 <= i < j < nums.length` such that `low <= (nums[i] XOR nums[j]) <= high`.
hints: countPairs(low, high) = countAtMost(high) - countAtMost(low - 1).
A binary trie of the numbers' bits lets you count, for each number, how many previously-inserted numbers XOR with it to a value at most X, in O(bit-length) per query.

test_cases.explanation: Every pair XORs to 0, all three pairs qualify.

title: Number of Good Ways to Split a String
description: Given a string `s`, a split at some position divides it into a non-empty left part and a non-empty right part, covering every character exactly once. The split is "good" if the number of distinct characters in the left part equals the number of distinct characters in the right part. Return the number of good splits.
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.
hints: Precompute, for every prefix, the number of distinct characters so far, and separately for every suffix. A split after index i is good exactly when those two counts match.

test_cases.explanation: Splitting into 'aac'/'aba' and 'aacab'/'a' both give 2 distinct characters on each side.

title: Car Fleet II
description: There are `n` cars on a straight, one-lane road, all traveling in the same direction, given by their positions `position` (strictly increasing) and speeds `speed`. When a faster car catches up to a slower one ahead of it, they merge into a fleet moving at the slower car's speed from then on. Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the time at which car `i` collides with the next car ahead of it (accounting for that car having possibly already slowed down after merging with one further ahead), or -1 if it never catches up to anyone.
hints: Process cars from right to left with a monotonic stack of 'still relevant' candidate collisions.
A car ahead that is slower can never be caught later than its OWN collision time with the car ahead of it -- pop candidates from the stack whose collision time is too late to matter.

test_cases.explanation: Car 0 catches car 1 at t=1; car 3 catches car 4 at t=2; cars 1, 2 and 4 never catch anyone ahead.
Equal speeds -- car 0 never catches car 1.

title: Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique Characters
description: Given an array of strings `arr`, return the length of the longest possible string you can form by concatenating some subset of `arr` (each used at most once, in any order) such that the result has no repeated characters. Any string in `arr` that already has a repeated character can never be used.
constraints: arr[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Represent each valid (no-internal-duplicate) string as a 26-bit character bitmask.
Backtrack over subsets: a candidate string can be added only if its bitmask shares no bits with the characters used so far.

test_cases.explanation: 'un'+'iq' or 'iq'+'ue' both give 4 unique characters ('un'+'iq'+'ue' would repeat 'u').
Both strings already contain a repeated character, so neither is usable.

title: Count Square Sum Triples
description: A square triple `(a, b, c)` is a triple of positive integers where `a^2 + b^2 == c^2`. Given an integer `n`, return the number of square triples such that `1 <= a, b, c <= n` (note that `(a, b, c)` and `(b, a, c)` are counted as two distinct triples when `a != b`).
hints: For every ordered pair (a, b), check whether a^2 + b^2 is a perfect square no greater than n^2 -- n is small enough that the O(n^2) double loop is intended.

test_cases.explanation: The only triples are (3,4,5) and (4,3,5).

title: Lemonade Change
description: At a lemonade stand, each lemonade costs $5. Customers pay with a $5, $10, or $20 bill, one at a time in the order given by `bills`, and you must give correct change from your current till (which starts empty). Return true if you can provide correct change to every customer.
hints: Only track how many $5 and $10 bills you're holding -- a $20 bill should always be broken using a $10+$5 first if possible (saving $5 bills, which are more flexible, for later).

test_cases.explanation: Change given: none, none, none, $5 back, then $15 back as a $10+$5.
By the last customer you have no $5 bills left to make $15 change.
No $5 bill has been received yet to make change for the first $10.

title: Maximum Units on a Truck
description: You are loading boxes onto a truck with capacity for `truckSize` boxes total. `boxTypes[i] = [numberOfBoxesi, numberOfUnitsPerBoxi]` describes one box type. Choose which boxes to load (up to `truckSize` boxes total) to maximize the total number of units carried, and return that maximum.
hints: Always fill the truck with the highest-units-per-box type available first -- sort box types by units-per-box descending and take greedily.

test_cases.explanation: Take the 1 box worth 3 units, then both boxes worth 2 units: 3+2+2=7.
Only 1 box exists, so at most 1 unit can be carried.

title: Minimum Platforms
description: A railway station has trains arriving and departing throughout the day, given by `arrival[i]` and `departure[i]` (both in 24-hour format as integers, with a train occupying its platform from its arrival time through its departure time inclusive). Return the minimum number of platforms required so that no two trains that need a platform at the same time ever share one.
hints: Sort arrivals and departures independently, then sweep both with two pointers like merging two sorted lists: an arrival needs a new platform, a departure frees one -- track the running count and its maximum.

test_cases.explanation: At time 950, three trains (arriving at 900,940,950) are all still present -- 3 platforms are needed.
All three trains overlap completely.

title: Job Sequencing Problem
description: You are given `n` jobs, each taking exactly one unit of time, with `deadlines[i]` (the job must finish by this time unit, counting from 1) and `profits[i]` (earned only if the job completes by its deadline). At most one job can run in any given time unit. Return `[count, totalProfit]`: the maximum number of jobs that can be scheduled and the total profit earned by that schedule.
hints: Sort jobs by profit descending, then greedily place each job in the LATEST still-free time slot at or before its deadline (this leaves earlier slots open for jobs with tighter deadlines).

test_cases.explanation: Job 0 (profit 20, deadline 4) and job 2 (profit 40, deadline 1) run -- 2 jobs, profit 60.
Only one slot exists, so only the most profitable job (15) can run.

title: Fractional Knapsack
description: Given the weights `weights[i]` and values `values[i]` of `n` items, and a knapsack of capacity `capacity`, you may take any fraction of an item (not just whole items). Return the maximum total value obtainable without exceeding the capacity.
hints: Since fractions are allowed, always take items in decreasing order of value-per-unit-weight -- take a whole item if it fits, otherwise take exactly the fraction that fills the remaining capacity, then stop.

test_cases.explanation: Take all of item 1 (60) and item 2 (100), then 2/3 of item 3 (80) for a total of 240.
Only one item exists and it fully fits -- value 10.
Half the item fits, giving half its value.

title: Check If It Is a Straight Line
description: Given an array of points `coordinates` on the X-Y plane where `coordinates[i] = [x, y]`, return true if all the points lie on a single straight line.
constraints: All the given points are distinct.
hints: Avoid dividing by zero: instead of comparing slopes with division, cross-multiply. A point (x,y) is on the line through (x0,y0) and (x1,y1) exactly when (x1-x0)*(y-y0) == (y1-y0)*(x-x0).

test_cases.explanation: Every point lies on y = x + 1.
A vertical line (x=0) is still a straight line.
(3,4) breaks the y=x pattern.

title: Valid Boomerang
description: Given three distinct points `points` on the X-Y plane, a boomerang is a set of points that are NOT all in a straight line. Return true if the given points form a boomerang.
constraints: All the given points are distinct.
hints: Three points are collinear exactly when the cross product of the two vectors from the first point to the other two is zero -- a valid boomerang is simply the non-collinear case.

test_cases.explanation: All three points lie on y = x -- collinear, not a boomerang.

title: Erect the Fence
description: You are given the positions of trees, `points[i] = [xi, yi]`, on a 2D garden. You want to build a fence using the minimum length of rope that encloses all the trees. Return the vertices of the convex hull enclosing all the trees, in any order. No three of the given points are collinear along a hull edge, so the hull's vertex set is unambiguous.
constraints: All the given points are distinct.
No three points that would lie on the hull boundary are collinear.
hints: This is the classic convex hull problem -- Andrew's monotone chain builds the lower and upper hulls in O(n log n) after sorting points by (x, y).

test_cases.explanation: The interior point (2,2) isn't part of the fence -- only the 4 square corners are.
All 3 points are needed to enclose the triangle.
A single tree needs no fence beyond itself.

title: Determine Color of a Chessboard Square
description: Given a square on an 8x8 chessboard identified by its algebraic notation `coordinates` (a letter 'a' to 'h' followed by a digit '1' to '8'), return true if the square is white (light), false if it is black (dark).
hints: Convert the letter to a 0-based column and the digit to a 0-based row; the square is white exactly when column + row is odd (since 'a1' is a dark square).

test_cases.explanation: a1 is a dark (black) square.
h3 is a light (white) square.

title: Max Consecutive Ones
description: Given a binary array `nums`, return the maximum number of consecutive 1's in the array.
hints: Keep a running streak counter that resets to 0 on every 0, tracking the best streak seen.

test_cases.explanation: The longest run of 1's has length 3.

title: Binary Watch
description: A binary watch has 4 LEDs on the top representing the hour (0-11) and 6 LEDs on the bottom representing the minute (0-59); each LED that is on represents one bit of the corresponding binary value. Given the number of LEDs that are currently on, `turnedOn`, return every possible time the watch could be showing, formatted as "H:MM" (no leading zero on the hour, always two digits for the minute), sorted in ascending chronological order.
hints: Just enumerate every (hour, minute) pair from 0-11 and 0-59, and keep the ones whose combined popcount equals turnedOn.

test_cases.explanation: 8 is the maximum achievable LED count: it pairs each 3-bit hour (7 or 11) with each 5-bit minute (31, 47, 55, or 59), giving 8 valid times.
No valid time uses 10 LEDs -- the maximum possible is 8 (3 for the hour's 11, 5 for the minute's 59).

title: The Number of Weak Characters in the Game
description: You are given a 2D array `properties`, where `properties[i] = [attacki, defensei]` describes the i-th character. A character is weak if there exists another character with BOTH strictly greater attack AND strictly greater defense. Return the number of weak characters.
hints: Sort by attack descending, breaking ties by defense ASCENDING (so same-attack characters never flag each other). Then scan once, tracking the maximum defense seen so far -- a character is weak exactly when its defense is less than that running maximum.

test_cases.explanation: (2,2) is weak because (3,3) has strictly greater attack AND defense.
(4,3) is weak because of (10,4); neither (1,5) nor (10,4) is weak.
